column1: # Syscall numbers, names, and the shape of what they are called with. x86-64.
# A copy of the table the syscall backend is built from, kept because that backend exists on one
# platform only and sits below a boundary this crate is above. scripts/lint-rules.sh compares the
# number and the name against the original and fails on any disagreement, so the copy cannot drift.
# Every number here is one this build has an opinion about, which by the rule that an unknown
# syscall stops a run rather than reaching the host is every number a stored trace can contain.
# **The third column is what makes a digest mean "the same run".** A syscall is entered with six
# registers whatever it takes, and what a call does not take holds whatever was there before — in a
# program the size of an execution client, a pointer. Two runs of one client under two memory
# footprints produced the same 36 735 events, in the same order, with the same returns, and 11 233
# differing lines, every one an argument register of a call that does not read it.
# One character per argument the call reads, in ABI order, and nothing for the registers after them:
#   s   a value the call reads as a value: a descriptor, a flag, a length, an offset, a signal
#   p   an address. Where it points is behaviour; what it equals is a fact about this run's memory
#   -   the call reads none of the six
# The classification follows each call's declared prototype rather than what a particular guest
# passes, so it is a fact about Linux and not about a target. A number absent from this table is
# hashed by all six registers, which is stricter than necessary and never wrong.
# The fourth column is what the filter does with the call: `trace` stops the guest and hands the
# call to the world, `admit` lets it through to the host. A call the world answers is one the filter
# traces, which a test of the world holds it to.
